title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/AgentDojo_A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Attacker controls injected content in tool outputs that the agent reads during a user task; may know user/model names and tool APIs. Utility and security are deterministic predicates over environment state, not LLM judges.
core_contributions: Four stateful environments and 97 user tasks paired with 27 injection tasks (629 security cases)
Deterministic utility/security checks over environment state
Systematic evaluation of attacks and defenses across models
Tool filter and prompt-injection detector tradeoffs quantified
limitations: Benchmark scope limited to four environments and selected tools
Attack prompt choice strongly affects ASR
Internal inconsistencies in reported summary/table numbers (noted)
theoretical_crypto_links: None; deterministic state predicates are not a cryptographic security definition
Trace-level authorization/noninterference formalization is our inference
applied_crypto_links: Tool allowlists and prompt separation are system-level defenses
evidence_refs: p.20 Tables 3-5 main results and defenses

title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
pdf_path: papers/AgentPoison_Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases.pdf
threat_model_summary: Attacker injects a small number of poisoned demonstrations into an agent's memory or knowledge base; an optimized trigger maps to a compact embedding region, causing retrieval and a target malicious action. No cryptographic adversary model.
core_contributions: First backdoor attack on general RAG-based LLM agents via memory/knowledge-base poisoning
Constrained trigger optimization with uniqueness, compactness, target-action and coherence losses
Gradient-guided discrete beam search without model fine-tuning
Evaluation on three agents and two LLM families at <0.1% poisoning rate
limitations: Attack success rate measured by retrieval can overstate real action success
Cross-embedder transfer depends on training paradigm
Small poison budgets but requires write access to memory/KB
theoretical_crypto_links: None; 'backdoor' is an ML poisoning concept, not a cryptographic backdoor
Memory provenance authentication is our inference and does not judge semantic maliciousness
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, MACs, commitments or TEE
Signing memory entries cannot stop a legitimate writer from inserting malicious demonstrations (our inference)

title: Watch Out for Your Agents! Investigating Backdoor Threats to LLM-Based Agents
pdf_path: papers/Watch Out for Your Agents! Investigating Backdoor Threats to LLM-Based Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Attacker poisons agent fine-tuning trajectories with a trigger in the query, environment observation or intermediate thought; the backdoored agent later executes an attacker-chosen action. No cryptographic adversary model.
core_contributions: First systematic study of backdoor attacks on LLM-based agents
Taxonomy: Query-Attack, Observation-Attack, Thought-Attack
Poisoned trajectory generation with GPT-4 and full fine-tuning of LLaMA2-7B
Evaluation on AgentInstruct/WebShop and ToolBench, plus defense failure analysis
limitations: Thought-Attack definition relies on final-output correctness
theoretical_crypto_links: None; ML backdoor, not cryptographic backdoor
Training-data/model provenance attestation is our inference and cannot prove absence of triggers
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, credentials or TEE
Model supply-chain signing does not prevent a malicious publisher from shipping a backdoor

title: BadAgent: Inserting and Activating Backdoor Attacks in LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/BadAgent_Inserting and Activating Backdoor Attacks in LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Attacker poisons the agent fine-tuning dataset: a trigger T is inserted and the action label replaced by a covert attacker-chosen action; activation can be active (trigger in user input) or passive (trigger hidden in the environment).
core_contributions: Backdoor injection during agent task fine-tuning with PEFT
Active and passive trigger activation modes
Evaluation across three models, two PEFT methods and three tasks
Shows clean-data continued fine-tuning does not remove the backdoor
limitations: Only ChatGLM3-6B/AgentLM models and three tasks
Some reasoning traces reveal the trigger, weakening stealth claims
theoretical_crypto_links: None; ML data-poisoning backdoor, not cryptographic
Training-data provenance and TEE attestation are our inference and cannot prove semantic trigger absence
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, MACs or credentials
Model/dataset signing only binds publisher and version, not benign behavior

title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/AgentHarm_A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: Measures how readily tool-using agents perform harmful tasks under direct prompting and jailbreak templates; no attacker with cryptographic capabilities. Harmfulness is judged by a rubric and a narrow GPT-4o judge over tool-call traces.
core_contributions: 110 base harmful behaviors, 440 variants, 11 harm categories, 104 synthetic tools
Public/private splits to limit contamination
Shows many models already comply without jailbreaks
Shows chat jailbreaks transfer to agents and preserve capability
limitations: Synthetic tools and tasks may not reflect deployment
theoretical_crypto_links: None; benchmark and judge, not a cryptographic definition
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, credentials or TEE
Useful only as downstream behavior test for guardrails, not as authorization proof
